fuller.text: This is a long, textbook-style survey by four machine learning researchers that tries to bring order to deep learning. Its model is Felix Klein's 1872 Erlangen Programme, which treated geometry as the study of properties that stay unchanged under some set of transformations. Those transformations are called the symmetries of the geometry. The authors call their own attempt Geometric Deep Learning, and they aim to derive network designs from first principles of symmetry and invariance.

fuller.text: The authors say deep learning today resembles nineteenth-century geometry: a zoo of network designs with few unifying principles. That makes it hard to see how methods relate, so the same ideas get reinvented and renamed in different fields. A shared framework, they argue, does two jobs. It gives one mathematical way to study CNNs, RNNs, graph networks and Transformers, and a principled recipe for building future architectures.

fuller.text: The starting point is learning in high dimensions, where each input is described by a very large number of values, called d. If all we assume is that the target function changes smoothly, the number of examples needed grows exponentially with d. Even for modest d, this could exceed the number of atoms in the universe, a problem known as the curse of dimensionality. Simple networks escape this only by assuming the function depends on a few simplified views of the input, which the authors call unrealistic for images, speech or chemistry.

fuller.text: The way out is to use the structure of the domain the data lives on, such as the pixel grid under an image. The first principle is symmetry: changes to the domain, like shifting an image, that should not change the answer. A function is invariant if its output ignores such a change, as when a classifier says "cat" wherever the cat sits. It is equivariant if its output shifts along with the input, the way a pixel-by-pixel outline of an object must move when the object moves.

fuller.text: Exact symmetry is too idealised, because real scenes bend and warp in small, local ways. Small warps should barely change the output, but they cannot be treated as true symmetries, since many small warps add up to a large one. Fourier methods, which break a signal into global waves, fail here: a tiny warp can change their output by a fixed amount, however small the warp. Wavelets, which use small localised patterns at many sizes, stay stable instead. This leads to the second principle, scale separation: build features locally at fine scales, then pass them up to coarser versions of the domain.

fuller.text: Putting these together gives the Geometric Deep Learning Blueprint, built from a few repeating blocks stacked in layers. A local equivariant layer, such as a convolution, respects the domain's symmetry and looks only at nearby points. A nonlinearity, a simple bent function applied at each point, is needed because a purely straight-line invariant function could only use averages, like an image's mean colour. A coarsening or pooling step shrinks the domain, widening how far each feature can see. A final global pooling layer is invariant and gives one answer for the whole input.

A final global pooling layer is invariant and gives one answer for the whole input.

fuller.text: The authors apply the blueprint to five kinds of domain: grids, groups, graphs, geodesics and gauges. Groups here mean spaces with global symmetries like the sphere, geodesics mean distances measured along curved surfaces, and gauges mean local reference frames on such surfaces. On a grid, they show that convolution emerges from the single demand of being linear and unaffected by shifts. On a graph, whose nodes come in no fixed order, the key symmetry is reordering the nodes, so results must not depend on that order.

fuller.text: Many familiar architectures then appear as special cases of the same recipe. CNNs use a grid with shift symmetry, and spherical CNNs use the sphere with rotations. Graph networks, Deep Sets and Transformers use reordering symmetry; a Transformer is a graph network that weighs every other node by learned importance. Gated recurrent networks such as the LSTM come out of demanding invariance to time warping, meaning stretching or squeezing of time.

fuller.text: A tour of applications shows these ideas at work. A graph network screening molecules helped show that Halicin, first meant for diabetes, is a potent antibiotic, even against some resistant bacteria. A graph network predicts travel times in Google Maps across several major cities. A CNN reading the 19 by 19 Go board was central to AlphaGo, which beat Lee Sedol.

fuller.text: The text is open about limits. Spectral graph methods, built on a graph version of Fourier analysis, are so sensitive to small changes that they fail when moving between different meshes or graphs. Common graph networks are no more powerful than the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, a classic method that cannot tell a six-node ring from two triangles. The LSTM result is only a class guarantee: a network trained on one time warping cannot simply be reused on another.

fuller.text: The main conclusion is that a large class of deep learning architectures in use can be derived from common geometric principles. Methods differ mainly in their choice of domain, symmetry and how they build each block. The authors study well-known architectures in depth rather than covering everything, hoping readers can apply the same principles to designs yet to come.

brief.text: This long text tries to bring order to deep learning, where computers learn patterns from many examples. The authors say the field has a zoo of designs but few shared rules. So the same ideas keep getting reinvented under new names. They borrow an old idea from geometry: study what stays the same when things change.

brief.text: The key idea is symmetry: a change that leaves something important untouched. For example, sliding a cat across a photo does not change that it is a cat. They show that many popular designs follow one shared blueprint built on such symmetries. They call this Geometric Deep Learning, and say it also offers a principled way to build future designs.
